mainTopic: Using money from selling holy items, who owns a synagogue and may sell it, and whether ירושלים was divided among the שבטים
overview: The משנה finishes its 'ladder of holiness' (רחוב → בית הכנסת → תיבה → מטפחות → ספרים → ספר תורה). Money from selling a holy item may only buy something holier, and leftover money follows the same rule. The גמרא first notes, in the name of רבי יוחנן, that the רחוב being holy is only the view of רבי מנחם בר יוסי. He holds this because the town prays there on fast days, while the חכמים say that occasional use creates no קדושה. Next, רבי יונתן limits the sale of a בית הכנסת to a village synagogue, since a city synagogue belongs to the whole public. רב אשי adds that a synagogue run under one leader's authority can still be sold. The גמרא defends רבי יונתן against two challenges from ירושלים: a sold synagogue, and a ברייתא about נגעים. This leads to a dispute between תנאים over whether ירושלים was divided among the שבטים, with אביי drawing a side lesson about guests and hosts. Finally, רבא begins to limit the משנה's rule to sales not made by the שבעה טובי העיר before the townspeople, and his statement continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Going up the ladder: from scrolls to a Torah
steps.stepSummary: The משנה finishes its list of upward purchases. Money from selling other holy items may buy ספרים (scrolls of נביאים and כתובים), and money from selling those scrolls may buy a ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: …they may buy scrolls (of נביאים and כתובים). If they sold scrolls, they may buy a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of the משנה's list of things a community may buy, going up step by step in holiness. The last two rungs are scrolls of נביאים and כתובים, and then a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the משנה (on the previous page), the ladder starts with the רחוב and climbs through בית הכנסת, תיבה, and מטפחות. Here it reaches the top: ספרים, and finally a ספר תורה, which is the holiest item on the list. Moving up is always allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Scrolls of נביאים and כתובים (not a ספר תורה)
A ספר תורה, the holiest item on the ladder

steps.confusionAlert: Here סְפָרִים does NOT mean 'books' in general. It means scrolls of נביאים and כתובים, which are holy but less holy than a ספר תורה.

phrases.english: they may buy scrolls.
phrases.notes: This finishes the line before: if they sold מטפחות (wrapping cloths), they may buy scrolls.

phrases.english: If they sold scrolls, they may buy a Torah scroll.
phrases.notes: The top rung of the ladder.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's upward list from the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money from selling scrolls of נביאים and כתובים may be used to buy a ספר תורה, because you may always go up in holiness.

steps.title: Going down the ladder is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states the reverse rule. Money from a holier item may never buy a less holy item, at any rung of the ladder, all the way down to the רחוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if they sold a ספר תורה, they may not buy scrolls. If they sold scrolls, they may not buy wrapping cloths. If they sold wrapping cloths, they may not buy an ark. If they sold an ark, they may not buy a synagogue. If they sold a synagogue, they may not buy a town square.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now walks back down the same ladder. At each step it says that you may NOT use the money to buy the item below.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the principle of מעלין בקודש ואין מורידין: you go up in holiness, never down. Once money carries the holiness of a higher item, spending it on a lower item would lower its holiness. That is forbidden even by a single rung.

keyTerms.meaning: The ark or chest where the scrolls are kept
The town square, used for public prayer on fast days
We raise in holiness and do not lower (the principle behind the list)

steps.whatToRemember: The full ladder from lowest to highest is רחוב → בית הכנסת → תיבה → מטפחות → ספרים → ספר תורה. You may go up, but never down.

phrases.english: But if they sold a Torah scroll,
phrases.notes: אֲבָל flips the direction: going up was allowed, but going down is not.

phrases.english: they may not buy scrolls.
If they sold scrolls, they may not buy wrapping cloths.
If they sold wrapping cloths, they may not buy an ark.
If they sold an ark, they may not buy a synagogue.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת — לֹא יִקְחוּ אֶת הָרְחוֹב.
phrases.english: If they sold a synagogue, they may not buy the town square.
phrases.notes: The bottom rung.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל אִם מָכְרוּ תּוֹרָה — לֹא יִקְחוּ סְפָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 1 in reverse. It forbids the downward direction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money from selling a holy item may not be used to buy anything of lesser holiness.

steps.title: The same rule applies to leftover money
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds that money left over after a permitted purchase keeps the same restriction.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the same applies to their leftover money.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds one more rule. If money is left over after buying a holier item, that leftover money also cannot be used for anything of lower holiness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think that once the main purchase is done, the extra money is 'free'. The משנה says no. The leftover money still carries the holiness of the original item that was sold. So it, too, may only go up the ladder.

keyTerms.meaning: And likewise; the same rule applies

steps.whatToRemember: The 'only go up' rule follows the money itself, including any leftovers.

phrases.english: And likewise with their leftover funds.
phrases.notes: The same rule covers money left over after they buy something.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the rule of steps 1 and 2 to leftover money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Leftover proceeds keep the same restriction as the original proceeds.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן says the משנה follows one תנא only
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's opening case about selling the רחוב. Through רבה בר בר חנה, רבי יוחנן says this anonymous משנה reflects only the view of רבי מנחם בר יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: 'Residents of a town who sold the town square…' רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: This is the view of רבי מנחם בר יוסי, stated anonymously.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting the first case of the משנה, where the town sold its רחוב. It then reports רבי יוחנן's claim that this ruling is not everyone's view; it belongs to one תנא, רבי מנחם בר יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally an anonymous משנה (סתם משנה) sounds like the accepted view of everyone. רבי יוחנן tells us that here the anonymous voice is really a single opinion. That sets up the disagreement in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Stated anonymously (his view was taught without his name)

steps.confusionAlert: The quote 'בני העיר שמכרו רחובה של עיר' is not a new case. It is the גמרא quoting the start of the משנה (from the previous page) so it can comment on it.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: בְּנֵי הָעִיר שֶׁמָּכְרוּ רְחוֹבָהּ שֶׁל עִיר.
phrases.english: 'Residents of a town who sold the town square…'
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting the first line of the משנה.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: זוֹ דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מְנַחֵם בַּר יוֹסֵי סְתִומְתָּאָה,
phrases.english: This is the statement of Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei, cited anonymously,
phrases.notes: The anonymous משנה is really this one תנא's opinion.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion by identifying who wrote the משנה's first ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's view that the רחוב has holiness, so that its sale money must buy a בית הכנסת, belongs to רבי מנחם בר יוסי.

steps.title: The חכמים: the town square has no holiness
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן finishes his statement: the חכמים disagree and hold that the רחוב has no קדושה at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the חכמים say: the town square has no holiness.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of רבי יוחנן's statement. It tells us the opposing view: the חכמים say the רחוב is not holy at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the רחוב has no קדושה, then money from selling it is ordinary money. It does not have to be used for a בית הכנסת and may be spent on anything. So the bottom rung of the משנה's ladder is disputed.

keyTerms.meaning: It has no aspect of; it carries no

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's first rung, the רחוב, is disputed. רבי מנחם בר יוסי says it has קדושה. The חכמים say it has none, so its sale money may be used freely.
steps.whyThisMatters: Since the majority usually decides the הלכה, this statement suggests the חכמים's view may be followed, even though the anonymous משנה seemed to say otherwise.

phrases.english: But the Rabbis say:
The town square has no sanctity.
phrases.notes: So money from selling it may be used for any purpose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יוחנן's statement by giving the opposing view to רבי מנחם בר יוסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the חכמים, the רחוב has no קדושה, so the restriction on its sale money does not apply.

steps.title: What is רבי מנחם בר יוסי's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מנחם בר יוסי holds that the רחוב has קדושה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מנחם בר יוסי, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי מנחם בר יוסי thinks the town square is holy. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5 we learned that the חכמים say the רחוב has no קדושה. So the גמרא wants to know what makes רבי מנחם בר יוסי think it does. This is a request for a reason, not an attack.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei,
what is his reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the opinion that step 4 attributed to רבי מנחם בר יוסי, now that step 5 has given the חכמים' opposing view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the רחוב would have any קדושה at all.

steps.title: People pray in the square on fast days
steps.stepSummary: The רחוב is holy because the community prays there on fast days and during the מעמדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the people pray in it on fast days and during the מעמדות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the town square is a place where the community prays at special times, so it has some holiness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On public fast days the whole town gathered in the square to pray. The local מעמדות groups also prayed there. Because real public prayer happens there, רבי מנחם בר יוסי treats the square as a place of prayer with קדושה.

keyTerms.meaning: Local groups who prayed and read Torah while their section of כהנים served in the בית המקדש

phrases.english: Since the people pray in it
phrases.notes: "It" means the town square.

phrases.english: on fast days and during the ma'amadot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Public prayer takes place in the רחוב on fast days and during the מעמדות, so it counts as a place of prayer.

steps.title: The רבנן: that use is only occasional
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the חכמים' reasoning: praying in the רחוב is only an occasional event, so it does not make the square holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? They say that is merely an occasional thing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the other side: the חכמים say people pray in the square only once in a while, so it never becomes a holy place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that people pray in the square sometimes. They disagree about whether occasional use is enough to create קדושה. The חכמים say a place becomes holy only through regular, set use.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, the majority opinion (the חכמים)

steps.whatToRemember: The argument about the רחוב depends on one question: does occasional prayer make a place holy? רבי מנחם בר יוסי says yes. The חכמים say no, because it is only אקראי.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
That is merely an occasional occurrence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing reasoning of the חכמים, in response to the reason given in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Occasional prayer does not create קדושה; only regular, set use does.

steps.title: Selling a synagogue applies only to villages
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that a sold בית הכנסת can buy a תיבה. Through רבי שמואל בר נחמני, רבי יונתן says this applies only to a village synagogue.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A בית הכנסת: they may buy a תיבה.' רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: they taught this only about a village synagogue.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה, about selling a synagogue. It quotes רבי יונתן, who says this rule only covers a village synagogue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a town may sell its בית הכנסת and use the money for a holier item like a תיבה. רבי יונתן narrows this: the rule works for a village synagogue, which belongs to the villagers. The next step explains why a city synagogue is different.

keyTerms.meaning: The ark that holds the ספר תורה
They taught this only regarding…, a formula that limits a rule

phrases.english: "A synagogue: they may buy an ark."
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
They taught this only
about a synagogue of villages,

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת שֶׁל כְּפָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the משנה's case of selling a בית הכנסת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's permission to sell a בית הכנסת applies only to a village synagogue.

steps.title: A city synagogue belongs to everyone
steps.stepSummary: A city synagogue cannot be sold, because people from outside come to it, so it belongs to the public at large.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a city synagogue, since people come to it from outside, they cannot sell it, because it belongs to the public.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן continues: a big-city synagogue cannot be sold by the townspeople, because visitors from everywhere use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The townspeople can sell only what is theirs. A city synagogue serves travelers and outsiders too, so it belongs to all of the public. The local residents therefore cannot sell it on their own.

keyTerms.meaning: From the outside world, from elsewhere
Belonging to the public at large

steps.confusionAlert: This is not about a city synagogue being holier. The issue is ownership: no single group owns it, so no one has the right to sell it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the basis in הלכה for treating large public synagogues differently from small local ones when it comes to selling them.

phrases.english: But a synagogue of cities,
since people come to it from the outside world,
they are not able to sell it,
because it is considered property of the public.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יונתן's statement by explaining why the city case is excluded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city synagogue cannot be sold, since it belongs to the general public.

steps.title: רב אשי's synagogue in מתא מחסיא
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that his synagogue in מתא מחסיא may be sold if he wishes, even though outsiders come to it, because they come on his terms.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: this synagogue of מתא מחסיא, even though people from outside come to it, since they come by my consent, if I want, I can sell it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds a further rule. If a synagogue is run under one leader's direction, outsiders using it does not make it public property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן's reason was that outsiders make the synagogue public. רב אשי says that is true only if the outsiders come on their own. If they come under the authority of the person who set up the synagogue, it still belongs to him, and he may sell it.

keyTerms.meaning: רב אשי's town, where he led the community
On my terms, by my consent

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
This synagogue of Mata Mechasya,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּמֵעָלְמָא אָתוּ לַהּ,
phrases.english: even though people from outside come to it,
since they come by my consent,
if I wish, I can sell it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי הַאי בֵּי כְנִישְׁתָּא דְּמָתָא מַחְסֵיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי יונתן's city rule: outside visitors do not make a synagogue public property if they come under the founder's authority.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A synagogue that outsiders attend under one leader's authority still belongs to that leader, and he may sell it.

steps.title: A Jerusalem synagogue was sold to רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells of a synagogue in ירושלים that was sold to רבי אליעזר for his private use. That seems to contradict רבי יונתן, since ירושלים is a city.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: רבי יהודה said, there was an incident with the synagogue of the טורסיים in ירושלים, which they sold to רבי אליעזר, and he used it for all his needs. But that was a city synagogue!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יונתן with a story. A synagogue in the big city of ירושלים was sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן said a city synagogue cannot be sold. Yet a synagogue in ירושלים, which is certainly a city, was sold and used for ordinary purposes. That seems to show city synagogues can be sold.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it…? Introduces the point of contradiction

phrases.english: They raised an objection: Rabbi Yehuda said:
There was an incident with the synagogue of the bronze workers
that was in Jerusalem
which they sold to Rabbi Eliezer
and he used it for all his needs,
But there it was a synagogue of cities!
phrases.notes: Here the גמרא itself is pointing out the contradiction.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי יונתן's rule from steps 9 and 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יונתן's rule that a city synagogue cannot be sold.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A synagogue in ירושלים, a city, was sold and used for private purposes, which shows city synagogues can be sold.

steps.title: It was a small synagogue the workers built
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the Jerusalem synagogue was small and was built by the bronze workers themselves, so it was theirs to sell.
steps.simpleTranslation: That one was a small synagogue, and they themselves built it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יונתן. The Jerusalem synagogue was a small, private one that belonged only to the workers who built it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן's rule depends on ownership. A big city synagogue belongs to the public. A small synagogue that a specific group built for itself still belongs to that group, even in a city, so they may sell it.
steps.whatToRemember: Whether a synagogue can be sold depends on who owns it. A village synagogue, or a small synagogue a group built for itself, can be sold by its owners. A large city synagogue that serves the general public cannot be sold.

phrases.english: That one was a small synagogue,
and they themselves built it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case (אוקימתא): the story involved a special kind of synagogue.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any synagogue in a city, including the one in ירושלים, is public property, so the story contradicts רבי יונתן.
steps.terutzMaskana: A small synagogue built by a specific group belongs to that group even in a city, so it can be sold; רבי יונתן's rule stands.

steps.title: A ברייתא about נגעים in ירושלים is brought as an objection
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: only a house that is 'your possession' can get צרעת, so houses in ירושלים cannot. רבי יהודה says he heard this rule only about the מקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: The verse says 'in a house of the land of your possession.' 'Your possession' can become impure with נגעים, but ירושלים cannot become impure with נגעים. רבי יהודה said: I only heard this about the place of the מקדש alone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a ברייתא that it will use to attack רבי יונתן's rule. This step sets up the source, and the actual attack comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse links צרעת of houses to private ownership ('your possession'). The first תנא says all of ירושלים belongs to everyone, so its houses cannot get צרעת. רבי יהודה narrows this exemption to the מקדש only.

keyTerms.meaning: Your possession, meaning privately owned property
Plagues of צרעת (here, צרעת that appears on houses)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
phrases.notes: A ברייתא is about to be quoted that challenges what was just said.

phrases.english: "In a house of the land of your possession" (ויקרא 14:34),
'your possession' becomes impure with plagues,
phrases.notes: Only privately owned houses

phrases.english: but Jerusalem does not become impure with plagues.
phrases.notes: Because ירושלים belongs to all of Israel

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: אֲנִי לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said: I did not hear
phrases.notes: He is reporting what his teachers told him

phrases.english: except about the place of the Temple alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving the Jerusalem synagogue story, the גמרא brings a new source to challenge רבי יונתן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יונתן's rule (step 10) that a city בית הכנסת belongs to the public
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Set up here and made explicit in step 15: רבי יהודה's limitation implies that synagogues in ירושלים are treated as privately owned.

steps.title: According to רבי יהודה, synagogues in ירושלים could become impure, but they belong to the city
steps.stepSummary: From רבי יהודה's words it follows that synagogues and study halls in ירושלים can become impure. But according to רבי יונתן they belong to the city, so why would they?
steps.simpleTranslation: This implies that synagogues and study halls do become impure. Why? They belong to the city!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from רבי יהודה's words and shows the problem it creates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only the מקדש is exempt, then synagogues in ירושלים can get צרעת, which means they count as privately owned. But רבי יונתן said that a city synagogue belongs to the whole public, and public property cannot get צרעת. So the inference clashes with his rule.

phrases.aramaic: הָא בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת מִיטַּמְּאִין,
phrases.english: This implies that synagogues and study halls become impure,
phrases.notes: An inference from 'only the Temple'

phrases.english: Why? They belong to cities!
phrases.notes: Uses רבי יונתן's principle that city synagogues are public

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת מִיטַּמְּאִין, אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the ברייתא into an explicit challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יונתן's ruling that city synagogues are public property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only private property can get צרעת. If city synagogues can get it, they are not public, which contradicts רבי יונתן.

steps.title: Fix the wording: רבי יהודה said 'a holy place,' not only the מקדש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes רבי יהודה's words from 'the place of the מקדש' to 'a holy place,' which includes synagogues and study halls.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: רבי יהודה said, I only heard this about a holy place alone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by correcting the text of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מִקְדָּשׁ ('Temple') is read as מְקוּדָּשׁ ('sanctified place'). Now רבי יהודה exempts every holy place in ירושלים from צרעת, including synagogues. This fits רבי יונתן's view that they are public.

keyTerms.meaning: A sanctified place (Temple, synagogues, study halls)

steps.confusionAlert: The two words look almost the same: מִקְדָּשׁ means the Temple, and מְקוּדָּשׁ means any holy place. The whole answer depends on that small change.

phrases.english: Say instead: Rabbi Yehuda said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנִי לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶלָּא מְקוֹם מְקוּדָּשׁ בִּלְבַד.
phrases.english: I did not hear except about a sanctified place alone.
phrases.notes: This includes synagogues and study halls

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהודה exempts only the מקדש, so synagogues in ירושלים are private.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה exempts all holy places, so synagogues are public, as רבי יונתן said.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle the first תנא and רבי יהודה argue about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is settled, and the גמרא now asks for the reason behind the dispute in the ברייתא. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first תנא exempts all of ירושלים, while רבי יהודה exempts only holy places. The גמרא wants the underlying principle that explains this difference.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending רבי יונתן to explaining the ברייתא's dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The principle that underlies the dispute between the first תנא and רבי יהודה

steps.title: Was ירושלים divided among the tribes?
steps.stepSummary: The first תנא holds that ירושלים was never given to any שבט. רבי יהודה holds that it was divided among the שבטים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first תנא holds that ירושלים was not divided among the tribes. רבי יהודה holds that ירושלים was divided among the tribes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by explaining the principle behind each opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ירושלים was never given to a שבט, then every house there belongs to all of Israel and cannot get צרעת. If it was divided, its houses are private, and only holy places belong to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (unnamed) opinion in the ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: The first תנא says ירושלים belongs to everyone, so none of its houses get צרעת. רבי יהודה says it was divided among the שבטים, so only holy places, including synagogues, are exempt.

phrases.english: The first tanna holds:
Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes,
phrases.notes: So it belongs to all of Israel

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yehuda holds:
Jerusalem was divided among the tribes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They argue about whether ירושלים was divided among the שבטים.

steps.title: This matches an older dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that these two views follow an earlier argument between other תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they follow the dispute of these תנאים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces another set of תנאים who argue about the same question. This step sets up the source that will be quoted next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question of whether ירושלים was divided among the שבטים is a known older dispute. Each side of the ברייתא lines up with one side of it.

phrases.english: And they follow the dispute of these tanna'im.
phrases.notes: The next source will quote that dispute

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links the dispute of step 18 to an earlier argument between תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The question of whether ירושלים was divided among the שבטים is itself an older dispute between תנאים.

steps.title: A ברייתא that splits the בית המקדש between יהודה and בנימין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists which parts of the בית המקדש were in יהודה's portion and which were in בנימין's portion. This shows that one תנא holds ירושלים was divided among the שבטים.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: What was in the portion of יהודה? The הר הבית, the chambers, and the courtyards. And what was in the portion of בנימין? The אולם, the היכל, and the קודש הקדשים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the first source for the earlier מחלוקת. This ברייתא assigns parts of the בית המקדש to specific שבטים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If parts of the בית המקדש belong to יהודה and parts belong to בנימין, then the land of ירושלים must have been divided among the שבטים. So this תנא holds like רבי יהודה's view from Step 18.

keyTerms.meaning: His portion, a שבט's share of land
Chambers or rooms in the בית המקדש
The courtyards of the בית המקדש
The Holy of Holies, the holiest room

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: מָה הָיָה בְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: As it is taught: What was in the portion of Judah?
The Temple Mount, the chambers, and the courtyards.
And what was in the portion of Benjamin?
The Entrance Hall, the Sanctuary, and the Holy of Holies.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: מָה הָיָה בְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first side of the earlier מחלוקת mentioned in Step 19.
steps.raayaObject: The view that ירושלים was divided among the שבטים
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא assigning parts of the בית המקדש to יהודה and to בנימין

steps.title: The strip of land with the מזבח and בנימין's longing for it
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא continues. A strip of יהודה's land reached into בנימין's portion, and the מזבח stood on it. בנימין longed every day to own it, so he was rewarded by hosting the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A strip of land went out from יהודה's portion into בנימין's portion, and the מזבח was built on it. The righteous בנימין was pained over it every day, wanting to take it in, as it says: 'He covers it all day long.' Therefore בנימין merited to become the host of the שכינה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a detail about the מזבח. It explains why בנימין was chosen to have the holiest part of the בית המקדש in his land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מזבח stood on יהודה's land, even though it stuck into בנימין's area. בנימין's strong longing for this holy spot is learned from the פסוק 'חופף עליו כל היום'. As a reward, the קודש הקדשים, where the שכינה rests, was in his portion.

keyTerms.meaning: A strip, a narrow piece of land
To swallow it up, to take it into his own portion
He covers it, he hovers over it (a פסוק in בנימין's ברכה)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two areas. The מזבח was NOT in בנימין's portion. It stood on a strip that belonged to יהודה. That is exactly why בנימין was pained over it.

phrases.aramaic: וּרְצוּעָה הָיְתָה יוֹצֵאת מֵחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: And a strip went out from the portion of Judah
and entered into the portion of Benjamin,
and on it the altar was built,
and Benjamin the righteous was pained over it
every day, wanting to take it in,
as it says: 'He covers it all day long,'
phrases.notes: דברים לג:יב, from משה's ברכה to בנימין

phrases.english: therefore Benjamin merited
and became the host of the Divine Presence.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּרְצוּעָה הָיְתָה יוֹצֵאת מֵחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with an aggadic detail about the מזבח and בנימין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מזבח stood on a strip of יהודה's land. Because בנימין longed for it, he merited that the קודש הקדשים would be in his portion.

steps.title: The other תנא: houses in ירושלים may not be rented out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא showing that another תנא holds ירושלים was never divided. Houses there may not be rented out because they don't belong to the people living in them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this other תנא holds that ירושלים was not divided among the שבטים. As it is taught: One may not rent out houses in ירושלים, because they do not belong to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now brings the source for the other side of the מחלוקת. This ברייתא shows that ירושלים belongs to all of כלל ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you cannot rent out your house in ירושלים, you must not truly own it. That only makes sense if ירושלים was never given to any שבט and belongs to the whole nation. This matches the view of the תנא קמא in Step 18.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main source for the view that ירושלים belongs to everyone. That idea is why the תנא קמא of the ברייתא about נגעים (step 14) holds that houses in ירושלים cannot become impure with צרעת like private houses.

phrases.english: And this tanna holds
Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes.
As it is taught: One may not rent out houses in Jerusalem,
because they do not belong to them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַאי תַּנָּא סָבַר לֹא נִתְחַלְּקָה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם לִשְׁבָטִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the second side of the מחלוקת, the opposite of Step 20.
steps.raayaObject: The view that ירושלים was not divided among the שבטים
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא forbidding renting out houses in ירושלים because the occupants do not own them

steps.title: Not even beds may be rented, so innkeepers take the hides by force
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בר צדוק adds that even beds may not be rented out in ירושלים. So when innkeepers take the hides of a guest's קרבנות, they are taking them by force.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בר צדוק says: Not even beds. Therefore, the hides of קדשים, the innkeepers take them by force.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues. רבי אלעזר בר צדוק widens the rule from houses to beds, and then draws a result about innkeepers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since an innkeeper in ירושלים may not charge rent for a room or even a bed, he has no right to payment. Guests usually left the hides of their קרבנות as payment. So when the innkeeper takes the hides, it is considered as if he takes them by force, without a real right to them.

keyTerms.meaning: Hides of animals brought as קרבנות

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok says:
Not even beds.
Therefore, the hides of sacrificial animals,
the innkeepers take them by force.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר (בַּר צָדוֹק) אוֹמֵר: אַף לֹא מִטּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, extending the rule against renting and adding a result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even beds may not be rented out in ירושלים. So innkeepers who take the hides of קדשים are taking them by force, without a right to payment.
steps.whatToRemember: Two ברייתות show the two sides. The first one splits the בית המקדש between יהודה and בנימין, so ירושלים was divided. The second one forbids renting out houses and beds, so ירושלים belongs to everyone.

steps.title: אביי's lesson: a guest should leave his flask and hide for his host
steps.stepSummary: Since the topic of inns came up, אביי learns from the ברייתא that it is good manners for a guest to leave his flask and the animal's hide with his host.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Learn from this that it is proper manners for a person to leave his flask and the hide at his host's place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a side lesson connected to the last ברייתא. אביי draws a rule of good manners from the innkeepers' practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows that guests were used to leaving the hides with their hosts. אביי learns from this that even when no payment is owed, it is proper to leave the host a gift, such as an empty wine flask and the hide of the animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Proper manners, the way of the world

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical lesson in דרך ארץ. A guest should show thanks to his host even when he is not required to pay.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Learn from this
that it is proper manners for a person to leave
his flask and the hide at his inn.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ אוֹרַח אַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side lesson drawn from the innkeepers mentioned in the ברייתא of Step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is proper manners for a guest to leave his flask and the animal's hide with his host.

steps.title: רבא limits the משנה's rule on selling a synagogue
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the משנה's limit on how sale money from a בית כנסת may be spent applies only when the שבעה טובי העיר did not sell it in front of the townspeople. If they did sell it that way, then 'even' (the sentence continues on the next amud) the usual limits do not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The משנה taught its rule only when the seven leaders of the town did not sell it in front of the people of the town. But if the seven leaders of the town did sell it in front of the people of the town, then even…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the side topic of ירושלים and goes back to the משנה. רבא narrows the משנה's rule, and this passage stops in the middle of his sentence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that money from selling a בית כנסת may only be used for something holier. רבא says this applies only to an ordinary sale. When the town's seven leaders sell in front of the townspeople, the sale has the full authority of the whole town, so the strict limit is removed. The word 'אפילו' tells us he is about to name something surprising that is allowed. That comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They only taught this when…' The phrase used to narrow an earlier teaching to a specific case.
The seven leaders chosen to run the town's affairs.
In the presence of the townspeople, meaning in a public assembly.
Even. It signals that a surprising case is coming.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבא is arguing with the משנה. He accepts it fully and only limits its scope. The strict rule stays in place for an ordinary sale. It only changes when the seven leaders sell with the town's backing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the practical guideline for how a community may use money from selling a בית כנסת. The full authority of the town's leaders, acting publicly, changes what the money may be spent on.

phrases.english: Rava said:
They taught this only
phrases.notes: This opening tells us a limit is being put on the משנה.

phrases.english: when the seven representatives of the town did not sell it
in an assembly of the residents of the town,
but if the seven representatives of the town did sell it
in an assembly of the residents of the town, then even…
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side topic of ירושלים and inns (steps 17–24) ends, the גמרא goes back to the משנה about selling holy items of the town.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's limits on using the money from selling a בית כנסת apply only when the sale was not made by the שבעה טובי העיר in a town assembly. A sale made that way is treated differently. The details continue after 'אפילו' on the next amud.
